facts.statement: In 1997, Rinchen Barsbold re-examined Oviraptor mongoliensis and determined it belonged to the new genus Rinchenia, though it remained an informal nomen dubium.

facts.statement: In 2018, Mark A. Norell and colleagues reported a new Oviraptor specimen, AMNH 33092, consisting of a tibia and two metatarsals from a juvenile or nestling.

facts.statement: Oviraptor likely had two well-developed hindlimbs ending in three functional toes, with the first toe being vestigial.
facts.quote: Though the holotype largely lacks the posterior region of the skeleton, it is likely that Oviraptor had two well-developed hindlimbs that ended in three functional toes with the first one being vestigial

facts.statement: Like related oviraptorids, Oviraptor had arms covered in elongated feathers and a tail ending in a pygostyle that supported a fan of feathers.
facts.quote: As evidenced in related oviraptorids, the arms were covered by elongated feathers, and the tail ended in a pygostyle, which is known to support a fan of feathers

facts.statement: The preserved skull of Oviraptor is deep, shortened, and measures approximately 17.9 cm in length.
facts.quote: The skull of Oviraptor was deep and shortened with large fenestrae (openings) compared to other dinosaurs, and measures about 17.9 cm (7.03125 in) long as preserved.

facts.statement: Although the holotype skull lacks a crest, bone surface evidence suggests Oviraptor likely possessed a well-developed crest supported by nasal and premaxilla bones.
facts.quote: The holotype skull lacks a crest in almost its entirety, however, the top surfaces of the fused parietal and frontal bones indicate that it likely had a well-developed crest, supported by the nasal and premaxilla bones (mainly the latter) of the rostrum.

facts.statement: Oviraptor had toothless jaws terminating in a robust, parrot-like horny beak called a rhamphotheca.
facts.quote: Oviraptor had toothless jaws that ended in a robust, parrot-like rhamphotheca (horny beak).

facts.statement: The lower jaw of Oviraptor is a short, deep bone measuring 19.5 cm in length.
facts.quote: As a whole, the lower jaw is a short and deep bone that covers 19.5 cm.

facts.statement: Oviraptor had three skinny, bird-like fingers, each ending in a side-to-side flattened and recurved claw.
facts.quote: The hand of Oviraptor had three skinny and bird-like fingers with each finger ended in side to side flattened and recurved unguals (claw bone).

facts.statement: A nest associated with Oviraptor preserves elongatoolithid eggs that are approximately 14 cm long.
facts.quote: The nest AMNH 6508 preserves elongatoolithid eggs, with each egg being 14 cm long (some are incomplete).

facts.statement: Henry Fairfield Osborn originally classified Oviraptor with ornithomimids because of its toothless beak.
facts.quote: Oviraptor was originally allied with the ornithomimids by Osborn due to its toothless beak.

facts.statement: In 1976, Rinchen Barsbold established the family Oviraptoridae, designating Oviraptor as its type genus.
facts.quote: In 1976, Barsbold erected a new family to contain Oviraptor and its close kin, making Oviraptor the type genus of the Oviraptoridae.

facts.statement: In 2002, Clark and colleagues redescribed the holotype skull of Oviraptor, noting its relatively elongated maxilla and dentary.
facts.quote: During the redescription of the holotype skull in 2002 by Clark and colleagues, they noted that Oviraptor had a relatively elongated maxilla and dentary.

facts.statement: In 1977, Rinchen Barsbold proposed that Oviraptor used its robust jaws and beak to crush mollusk shells like clams found in its geological formation.
facts.quote: In 1977, Barsbold proposed a crushing jaw hypothesis. He argued that the strength of the robust lower jaws and likely rhamphotheca (horny beak) was strong enough to break the shells of mollusks such as clams, which are found in the same geological formation as Oviraptor.

facts.statement: In 1990, David K. Smith rejected the crushing jaw hypothesis, arguing that Oviraptor's jaws preserved shearing surfaces rather than crushing mechanisms.
facts.quote: In a 1990 conference abstract, David K. Smith presented an osteological reevaluation of Oviraptor where he rejected the statements made by Barsbold. He found no evidence indicating a forelimb specialized in aquatic locomotion, and the jaws, rather than preserve a crushing mechanism, preserve shearing surfaces.

facts.statement: In 1995, Mary H. Norell and colleagues found lizard remains in the holotype's body cavity, suggesting Oviraptor was partially carnivorous.
facts.quote: However, in 1995, Norell and colleagues reported the fragmented remains of a lizard in the body cavity of the holotype specimen, suggesting that Oviraptor was partially carnivorous.

facts.statement: Stig Olav K. Jansen suggested Oviraptor was omnivorous, using its beak and forelimbs to catch and tear small prey.
facts.quote: Jansen suggested that oviraptorids were omnivorous as the sharply developed rhamphotheca together with the prominent forelimbs would have been adapted to catch and tear small prey.

facts.statement: When described in 1924, Oviraptor was presumed to be ovivorous (egg-eating) based on its discovery at a Protoceratops nest.
facts.quote: When first described in 1924 by Osborn, Oviraptor was originally presumed to have been ovivorous—an organism that has an egg-based diet—based on the association of the holotype with a nest thought to belong to Protoceratops.

facts.statement: Rinchen Barsbold suggested Oviraptor had a semiaquatic lifestyle based on its diet and anatomy, a hypothesis later contested by others.
facts.quote: Barsbold also suggested that oviraptorids could have had a semiaquatic life-style based on the mollusk-based diet, the high location of nasal cavities, an augmented musculature of the tail, and the greater size of the first manual digit.

facts.statement: Stig Olav K. Jansen considered Oviraptor's lower jaws strong enough to crush eggs, nuts, or hard seeds, suggesting an omnivorous diet.
facts.quote: However, he considered the lower jaws strong enough to have at least crushed elements like eggs, nuts or other hard seeds.

facts.statement: Traits of the Oviraptor skull suggest it belongs near the base of the Oviraptoridae family tree, distinct from more derived members.
facts.quote: During the redescription of the holotype skull in 2002 by Clark and colleagues, they noted that Oviraptor had a relatively elongated maxilla and dentary. These traits are less pronounced in derived oviraptorids and suggests that Oviraptor belongs to the near base of the Oviraptoridae.

facts.statement: Research since 1994 indicates that oviraptorids were not egg-eaters but instead brooded and cared for their nests.
facts.quote: Since the description of the embryonic Citipati specimen in 1994, oviraptorids became more understood: instead of having been egg-eating animals, they actually brooded and cared for the nests.

facts.statement: Researchers Dong and Currie suggested that a nesting oviraptorid specimen was caught and buried by a sandstorm while incubating eggs.
facts.quote: Dong and Currie suggested that it was caught and buried by a sandstorm during incubation.

facts.statement: Dong and Currie ruled out the hypothesis that oviraptorids were egg-thieves because such animals would have consumed or abandoned the nest before burial by a sandstorm.
facts.quote: They ruled out the possibility of oviraptorids being egg-thieves as they would have either consumed or instinctively abandoned the nest long before it was buried by a sandstorm or another meteorological phenomenon.

facts.statement: In 2005, Tamaki Sato and colleagues reported an oviraptorid specimen from the Nanxiong Formation that preserved the pelvic region with two eggs inside.
facts.quote: In 2005, Tamaki Sato and team reported an unusual oviraptorid specimen from the Nanxiong Formation.

facts.statement: Evidence from egg size and position suggests that oviraptorids had two functional oviducts but typically ovulated only one egg per oviduct.
facts.quote: The size and position of the eggs suggest that oviraptorids retained two functional oviducts, but had reduced the number of eggs ovulated to one per oviduct.

facts.statement: Persons and colleagues (2014) suggested that oviraptorosaurs were secondarily flightless and that tail traits may have been used for courtship displays.
facts.quote: In 2014, W. Scott Persons and colleagues suggested that oviraptorosaurs were secondarily flightless and several of the traits in their tails may indicate a propensity for display behaviour, such as courtship display.

facts.statement: Yang and colleagues (2018) identified cuticle layers on oviraptorid eggshells composed mainly of lipids and hydroxyapatite.
facts.quote: In 2018, Tzu-Ruei Yang and colleagues identified cuticle layers on several egg-shells of maniraptoran dinosaurs including those of oviraptorids.

facts.statement: Yang and colleagues suggested that the lipid-rich cuticle on oviraptorid eggs was an adaptation for hatching success in the arid, caliche-based environments where fossils are found.
facts.quote: As most oviraptorid specimens have been found in formations of caliche-based sedimentation, Yang and colleagues suggested that the cuticle-coated eggs would have been a reproductive strategy adapted for enhancing their hatching success in such arid climates and environments.

facts.statement: Oviraptor is known from the Bayn Dzak locality of the Djadokhta Formation in Mongolia, dating to the Late Cretaceous between 71 and 75 million years ago.
facts.quote: Oviraptor is known from the Bayn Dzak locality of the Djadokhta Formation in Mongolia, a formation that dates back to the Late Cretaceous about 71 million to 75 million years ago.

facts.statement: The Djadokhta landscape featured intermittent streams, seasonal moisture, and was occasionally affected by dust and sandstorms.
facts.quote: The semiarid steppe landscape was drained by intermittent streams and was sometimes affected by dust and sandstorms, and moisture was seasonal.

facts.statement: Climate in the region is thought to have shifted to a more humid fluvial environment during the later Campanian and Maastrichtian ages.
facts.quote: it is thought that later in the Campanian age and into the Maastrichtian, the climate would shift to the more humid fluvial environment seen in the Nemegt Formation.

facts.statement: Oviraptor remains come from the Bayn Dzak member of the Djadokhta Formation, which also yielded Bainoceratops, Pinacosaurus, Protoceratops, Saurornithoides, Velociraptor, and Halszkaraptor.
facts.quote: The known remains of Oviraptor have been produced by the Bayn Dzak member, which has also yielded the dinosaurs Bainoceratops, Pinacosaurus, Protoceratops, Saurornithoides, Velociraptor, and Halszkaraptor.

facts.statement: The Ukhaa Tolgod locality within the Bayn Dzak member has yielded Apsaravis, Byronosaurus, Citipati, Gobipteryx, Khaan, Kol, Shuuvuia, Tsaagan, and Minotaurasaurus.

facts.statement: The holotype of Oviraptor was likely trapped over a nest during a sandstorm, leading to rapid burial before scavenging or disarticulation could occur.
